script:
Now turn to Part two. You will hear a woman welcoming new volunteers to a community garden. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to twenty.
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Fenwick Community Garden. I'm Priya, and I coordinate the volunteers here. I'll take about ten minutes to tell you how the garden runs, and then we'll walk round it together.
First, the practical things. We are open every day from eight in the morning until dusk, but volunteer sessions are on Tuesdays and Saturdays only. Tuesday sessions run from ten until one. Saturday sessions are longer, from nine until three, and lunch is provided on Saturdays but not on Tuesdays, so bring something with you if you come midweek.
You will have seen the sign-in book by the gate. Please use it every time. It is not for checking up on anyone; it is what our insurance requires, and if the book says nobody is here, then officially nobody is here.
Now, the tools. The shed is unlocked during sessions and the code is only given to session leaders, so please don't take tools home even overnight. Everything comes back to the shed clean. There is a brush and a bucket by the door for that. The one thing I ask you to be careful with is the rotavator, which is heavy and is used by trained volunteers only.
About the plots. The garden is divided into three areas. The beds nearest the gate are the community beds, and everything grown there is shared. The middle section is the orchard, which needs almost nothing from us except in autumn. The far end is the wildlife area, and that one is deliberately left rough. Please don't tidy it. Every year somebody weeds it with the best intentions, and every year we lose the frogs.
We do ask for one thing that surprises people. If you take vegetables home, write them in the produce book. We are not counting what anyone takes, and there is no limit. We report the total weight to the council, and that figure is what keeps our lease at a peppercorn rent.
Finally, the children's sessions. Those run in the school holidays, on Wednesday mornings, and we need two extra adults each time. If you'd like to help with those, speak to Marcus rather than to me. He organises them and I never know the dates until he tells me.

items.stem: Community garden — length of Saturday sessions:
items.rationale: Two session times are given in the same passage and the candidate must take the second.

items.stem: On which day is lunch provided?
items.rationale: The speaker states lunch is provided on Saturdays and not on Tuesdays, and then repeats the point as advice.

items.stem: Community garden — where volunteers sign in:
items.rationale: The location is given once and the reason for signing in takes up the rest of the paragraph.

items.stem: Why must volunteers sign in?
items.rationale: The speaker rules out the checking-up reading explicitly and gives insurance as the reason.

items.stem: Community garden — who knows the shed code:
items.prompt: The code is given to ___ leaders only
items.rationale: The rule about the code is followed immediately by the rule about taking tools home, which is the more memorable instruction.

items.stem: Community garden — the tool restricted to trained volunteers:
items.rationale: One named tool is singled out at the end of a paragraph about tools in general.

items.stem: What is grown in the beds nearest the gate?
items.rationale: Three areas are described in order and only the first is the shared community beds.

items.stem: Community garden — the area that must be left alone:
items.rationale: The instruction is given with a reason attached, which is what makes it memorable and testable.

items.stem: Why is produce recorded?
items.rationale: The speaker denies both counting and limiting, and gives the council report and the rent as the reason.

items.stem: Community garden — who to ask about children's sessions:
items.prompt: Speak to ___ about the children's sessions
items.rationale: The speaker directs listeners away from herself, which is the point of the item.

script:
Now turn to Part two. You will hear a man explaining the arrangements at a residents' car park. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to twenty.
Good evening. Thank you for coming. I'm the building manager, and I've called this meeting because the car park arrangements change on the first of next month, and I would rather explain them now than answer forty emails afterwards.
Here is what is changing and, just as importantly, what is not. The number of spaces is not changing. There are fifty-two, there have always been fifty-two, and nobody is losing a space. What changes is how they are allocated.
Until now, spaces have been numbered and each flat has had its own. That sounds fair and it has not worked, because about a third of the spaces stand empty on any given day while visitors circle the block. From the first, the parking becomes unnumbered. You park in any space that is free, and your permit is what entitles you to be there rather than a particular rectangle of tarmac.
Permits arrive by post next week. Each flat gets one as before. If you want a second, there is a waiting list, and I will be honest with you: it is nineteen names long and it moves about twice a year.
The eight spaces along the north wall are the exception. Four of those are accessible bays and stay reserved, and they are enforced. The other four become visitor spaces, bookable through the building app for up to four hours. You book them under your own flat number, so if a visitor overstays it is your permit that gets the notice.
Charging points. There are two, and they are staying where they are, but the rule around them changes. At present people leave a car on a charger overnight. From the first, a charging bay is for three hours, and after that it is an ordinary space and you may be asked to move.
One more thing, and it is the one that will cause the most argument. The old numbered spaces near the lift were the ones everyone wanted, and under the new system nobody owns them. They will go to whoever arrives first. I know that is not popular with the people who have had them for years, but the alternative is keeping a system where a third of the tarmac sits empty and our visitors park on the street.

items.stem: Car park — total number of spaces:
items.rationale: The number is repeated twice in one sentence, which is the confirmation the item relies on.

items.stem: What is changing on the first of the month?
options: The size of the car park
items.rationale: The speaker separates what is not changing from what is, and only allocation is in the second list.

items.stem: Car park — proportion of spaces empty on a typical day:
items.rationale: The figure is given as the reason for the change and is repeated in the closing paragraph.

items.stem: Car park — when permits arrive:
items.rationale: The timing sits between two other pieces of information about permits.

items.stem: Car park — length of the second-permit waiting list:
items.rationale: The number is given with a frankness marker before it, which draws attention to the sentence but not necessarily to the figure.

items.stem: How many bays stay reserved for accessible parking?
items.rationale: Eight spaces are described along the north wall and they are split into two groups of four.

items.stem: Car park — maximum visitor booking:
items.prompt: Visitors may book for up to ___ hours
items.rationale: Two durations appear in the passage and this one belongs to visitor bookings rather than to charging.

items.stem: Who receives the notice if a visitor overstays?
items.rationale: The speaker explains that bookings are made under a flat number and that the permit holder gets the notice.

items.stem: Car park — new time limit at a charging point:
items.rationale: The old practice is described first, so a candidate must take the new rule rather than the habit.

items.stem: How will the spaces near the lift be allocated?
items.rationale: The speaker says nobody owns them and they go to whoever arrives first, then acknowledges the objection.

script:
Now turn to Part two. You will hear a woman describing a summer activity programme for teenagers. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to twenty.
Hello, and thanks for coming along this evening. I run the summer programme at the sports centre, and this is the meeting where parents ask me the questions the leaflet doesn't answer.
The programme runs for six weeks. It starts on the eighth of July. It is for young people between twelve and sixteen. We take a maximum of sixty a week. The first two weeks fill up. The last one stays quiet. So if you have any choice, book late rather than early.
The day starts at nine and finishes at four. We supervise from half past eight and until half past four. There is no extra charge for that. It is there because most of you work. Beyond those hours we cannot supervise. I would rather say that plainly now.
The activities split into three strands. Water sports are on Mondays and Wednesdays. They take place at the reservoir, not here. There is a coach at half past eight. It does not wait. Court sports are Tuesdays and Thursdays and are here in the main hall. Fridays are the trip day, and the destination changes each week.
About cost. The week costs ninety-five pounds. That includes everything except the Friday trip. A trip costs between ten and twenty-five pounds. It depends where we go. You pay for it on the Monday of the same week. If a trip is cancelled for weather, you are refunded in full.
Lunch is not provided. There is a canteen and it is reasonable, but many young people bring their own, and there is a fridge they may use. We ask that nothing containing nuts comes into the building at all.
Now the question everybody asks. Yes, they can leave at lunchtime if you have signed the form. No, we cannot let them go without it. A phone call from you on the day is not enough. The form has to be signed once, at the start, and it lasts the whole summer.
Bookings open on the fourteenth of May at nine in the morning, online only. We do not take bookings by phone, and I am afraid we cannot hold a place for anyone, including for the families who came last year.

items.stem: Summer programme — number of weeks:
items.rationale: The duration and the start date are given in the same sentence, so two numbers compete.

items.stem: Summer programme — maximum places per week:
items.rationale: The number is followed immediately by advice about booking, which is the more useful information and the distraction.

items.stem: What does the speaker advise about booking?
items.rationale: She explains that early weeks fill and the last is quiet, and draws the conclusion for the listener.

items.stem: Summer programme — earliest supervised drop-off:
items.rationale: Four times appear in one paragraph and only one is the start of supervision.

items.stem: Where do water sports take place?
items.rationale: The speaker states the location is not the centre and adds the coach time, which is the detail that follows.

items.stem: Summer programme — cost of one week:
items.rationale: Three sums appear in the paragraph and only this one is the weekly fee, which is given as a hyphenated number.

items.stem: When is the Friday trip paid for?
options: On the Monday of that week
At the end of the summer
items.rationale: The payment timing is given after the price range, which is where attention usually goes.

items.stem: Summer programme — food that is banned:
items.prompt: Nothing containing ___ may be brought in
items.rationale: The rule closes a paragraph about lunch arrangements and is the only prohibition in it.

items.stem: What allows a young person to leave at lunchtime?
items.rationale: The speaker gives both the yes and the no, and states that a call is not sufficient.

items.stem: Summer programme — when bookings open:
items.prompt: Bookings open on the ___ of May
items.rationale: Two dates appear in the passage, one for the start of the programme and one for booking.

script:
Now turn to Part two. You will hear a man briefing new staff at a hotel on their first morning. First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to twenty.
Good morning. I'm the duty manager, and this is the half hour where I tell you the things that are not in the handbook, or that are in it and get missed.
Start with your shifts. Early is seven until three, late is three until eleven, and you will be on a rota that changes every fortnight. The rota goes up on the Thursday before it starts. If you need a day, ask before the Thursday, because after it goes up I can only swap you with somebody who agrees.
Uniform. Shirts and aprons are provided and laundered here. Shoes are yours, and they must be closed at the toe. That is a kitchen rule that we apply everywhere, because everyone crosses the kitchen at some point.
Breaks. On an eight-hour shift you get one hour, and it is paid. Take it in the staff room on the second floor, not in the guest areas, and not at the back door, which is where people used to go and where guests can see you.
Now, the two rules I will not bend. The first is the key cards. Yours opens the rooms on your floor and the store cupboards. It does not open the office or the cellar, and if you find that it does, tell me, because that is a mistake and not a promotion. The second is the fire doors. They are held open by magnets and they close when the alarm sounds. Do not prop them, ever, not even for two minutes while you move a trolley.
About guests, one piece of advice rather than a rule. If a guest asks you something you do not know, do not guess. Say you will find out and then actually find out. Nearly every complaint I deal with started as a small wrong answer given confidently.
Finally, pay and problems. Pay goes in on the twenty-eighth, or the Friday before if that falls at a weekend. If something is wrong with it, come to me the same day, because the payroll cut-off is the third of the month and after that a correction waits until the next run.

items.stem: Hotel induction — end of the early shift:
items.rationale: Four times are given in one sentence, and this one is both the end of one shift and the start of another.

items.stem: Hotel induction — when the rota is published:
items.prompt: Rota goes up on the ___ before
items.rationale: The day is stated and then repeated as the deadline for requests.

items.stem: What must staff provide themselves?
items.rationale: Three items are named and the speaker separates what the hotel supplies from what it does not.

items.stem: Hotel induction — where breaks are taken:
items.rationale: The place is followed by two places where breaks may not be taken, which is the distraction.

items.stem: What does a staff key card NOT open?
items.rationale: The speaker lists what the card opens and then what it does not, and asks staff to report the exception.

items.stem: Hotel induction — what to do if a card opens too much:
items.rationale: The speaker identifies himself at the start and refers back to that role here.

items.stem: What is said about the fire doors?
options: They open with a key card
items.rationale: The instruction is absolute and the speaker names the excuse he is refusing.

items.stem: Hotel induction — advice about a question you cannot answer:
items.rationale: The advice is stated as an instruction and then explained through the complaints that follow from ignoring it.

items.stem: Hotel induction — pay date:
items.rationale: The date is qualified immediately by the weekend rule, which is where attention moves.

items.stem: Hotel induction — payroll cut-off:
items.rationale: Two dates about pay appear in the same paragraph and the question asks for the second.
